video_title: This Selloff Sets Up the Next Run For Bitcoin with Dylan LeClair
gist: Dylan LeClair of MetaPlanet argues the ~9-12 month drawdown in Bitcoin and Bitcoin treasury companies is a repeat of the 2021-22 sentiment washout, not a broken thesis: Strategy's preferreds were priced at credit-card-like yields despite $30B of Bitcoin net of liabilities, and convertible-bond delta decay — not fundamentals — is what squeezed the preferred stack. He details MetaPlanet's pivot from 'company that buys Bitcoin' to a Japanese neo-financial institution: acquiring MetaPlanet Securities (type-one license) to pioneer a high-yield credit market in a country with ~$7 trillion of cash earning zero and essentially no high-yield bond market, while planning Japan's first perpetual preferred. He says the bottom is likely in, attributing the low to quarter-end 13F window dressing that rotated hot money out of Bitcoin names into AI/memory stocks.

insights.claim: Dylan LeClair says the current 'Bitcoin treasury companies are dead' narrative is a near-exact repeat of the 2021-2022 cycle when Wall Street Journal articles declared Michael Sailor's strategy failed and predicted he would sell all his Bitcoin — which never happened.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Treat the current capitulation in BTC-treasury equities as a recurring cycle phase rather than a structural break; prior analogue resolved with a violent re-rating higher.
insights.quote: Michael Sailor in 2021 was like the the hero and then all of a sudden you know Wall Street Journal articles and the strategy failed and it's over and he's going to sell all his Bitcoin and and that didn't happen right

insights.claim: LeClair calls the market's recent pricing of Strategy's obligations irrational: the company holds $30 billion of Bitcoin net of all liabilities, yet three weeks prior the market was pricing its preferreds at credit-card interest rates.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: If the mispricing corrects, the Strategy preferred stack offers both a high running yield and price recovery — LeClair frames it as the clearest asymmetry in the complex.
insights.quote: Strategy has $30 billion of Bitcoin after all of its liabilities and the market three weeks ago said it's not worth credit card interest rates.

insights.claim: LeClair argues that a 50% Bitcoin drawdown mechanically forces levered Bitcoin equities to underperform, so their recent underperformance falsifies nothing about the thesis — only a 5-to-10-year period of no Bitcoin appreciation would.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Sets an explicit falsification horizon for the treasury-company trade: judge on 5-10 year Bitcoin performance, not 12-month drawdowns.
insights.quote: If Bitcoin goes down 50% and you're levered to Bitcoin, you're going to underperform. But conversely

insights.claim: LeClair says Bitcoin maximalists who treat Michael Sailor and Bitcoin-adjacent equities as the enemy are mistaken, because reaching a $100 trillion Bitcoin market cap requires Bitcoin merging into capital markets rather than retail sat-stacking alone.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Frames financialization products (preferreds, credit wrappers) as the demand channel for the next order of magnitude — a bullish read on issuers building those rails.
insights.quote: Bitcoin winning means Bitcoin and the capital markets merging. Um that was always the endgame.

insights.claim: Sentiment across Bitcoin and Bitcoin-adjacent investments is in the gutter after roughly nine to twelve months of straight-down price action from the all-time highs, with consensus on crypto Twitter believing Strategy would market-sell hundreds of thousands of Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Positions extreme insider-community bearishness as a contrarian sentiment indicator near a cycle low.

insights.claim: There are only five listed preferred securities in the entire Japanese stock market and none of them are perpetual, so MetaPlanet's stated plan to list a perpetual preferred would be a first for Japan.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: First-mover advantage in an untapped instrument class; success would open a domestic capital pool no other Bitcoin issuer can currently reach.
insights.quote: There are five listed preferred in the entire Japanese stock market.

insights.claim: Japan has no high-yield bond market at all — average corporate credit spreads are so tight that issuers price at 2-3%, making the market for 5-6% debt completely barren and, in LeClair's view, MetaPlanet's opening to pioneer it.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Identifies a structurally empty market segment; whoever builds the issuance and distribution rails captures the spread and the franchise value.
insights.quote: the market for high yield as in five to 6% debt is completely barren. It's open.

insights.claim: MetaPlanet acquired 100% of C SIBO Securities — now MetaPlanet Securities — a corporate bond brokerage that placed roughly 100 bond issues from about 40 issuers over six years at credit spreads of about 500 basis points over the Japanese government rate.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Gives concrete evidence the high-yield demand already exists in Japan at US-comparable spreads — the missing piece was a licensed distribution platform.
insights.quote: those those credit spreads meaning how additional what additional yield on top of the Japanese government rate was about 500 basis points

insights.claim: The MetaPlanet Securities type-one license lets MetaPlanet act as both direct issuer and neutral platform for other issuers, with the explicit goal of being the hub where the next wave of Bitcoin treasury companies raises capital in the 2027-2028 bull market.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Reframes MetaPlanet from a levered Bitcoin proxy into a fee-and-spread financial platform — a different valuation model than mNAV.

insights.claim: LeClair cites $7 trillion of cash sitting in Japan earning zero as the addressable pool MetaPlanet Securities is built to tap.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Quantifies the total addressable market for yen-denominated Bitcoin-linked yield products.
insights.quote: there's $7 trillion of cash in Japan earning zero

insights.claim: The MetaPlanet Securities business model is a net interest margin trade: buy a 13% dollar instrument, hedge it into yen at roughly 10% given the ~3% yen-dollar rate differential, add downside or credit protection, pay the Japanese investor 5% and keep about 3%.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: A concrete, repeatable earnings engine independent of Bitcoin price direction — the key to funding dividends without dilution.
insights.quote: we'll take the 13. we'll hedge it into yen at 10

insights.claim: Japanese investors treat anything yielding above 6% as too risky, which caps what MetaPlanet can offer domestically and drives the hedging-and-repackaging structure rather than direct pass-through of US preferred yields.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Explains why the Japan opportunity is a manufacturing/spread business rather than simple distribution — margin accrues to the packager.
insights.quote: Above six and people are going to say, I don't want anything to do with it. That looks too risky.

insights.claim: Japan's shareholder-communication infrastructure is still physical — MetaPlanet mails 250,000 paper notices across the island chain — so monthly or daily dividends of the kind US issuers offer are not yet operationally possible there.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: A real timing constraint on MetaPlanet's preferred roadmap; watch for tokenization/stablecoin settlement as the workaround that unblocks it.
insights.quote: There's 250,000 Manila envelopes that are sent across the island chains.

insights.claim: MetaPlanet reports 2.8 billion of Bitcoin against roughly 500 million of liabilities, leaving about $2 billion of net liquid collateral — which LeClair calls one of the strongest balance sheets among Japanese public companies excluding banks.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Sets the leverage baseline for judging solvency claims against headline mark-to-market losses in Japanese quarterly filings.
insights.quote: we have 2.8 billion of Bitcoin and, you know, 500 million and change of liabilities, right? So, net of that, we still have $2 billion of of liquid capital collateral

insights.claim: MetaPlanet runs an options-selling income strategy on roughly 2% of net assets that generated about $50 million over the last 12 months, intended to service dividends and interest with cash flow instead of equity dilution.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Directly answers the common-shareholder dilution objection with a measurable cash-flow number to track quarter over quarter.
insights.quote: it made I think about 50 million over the last 12 months

insights.claim: LeClair explicitly disagrees with Parker Lewis's claim that Bitcoin treasury companies must underperform Bitcoin because of dividend and interest costs, calling it a false equivalence — a levered issuer outperforms as long as Bitcoin outpaces its cost of capital.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: The debate reduces to a single testable variable: Bitcoin CAGR versus blended cost of capital on the preferred stack.
insights.quote: If you're a levered Bitcoin equity like you Strive, which Parker has been, you know, I I've seen him and Matt Cole go back and forth.

insights.claim: About 60% of Strive's BTC NAV has preferred issued against it, which LeClair says means Strive and MSTR would both outperform Bitcoin in a doubling scenario.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Quantifies the embedded leverage that determines upside beta in the next Bitcoin advance.
insights.quote: they're I think like 60% of their BTC nav is that has preferred issued against it.

insights.claim: Over roughly 12 months including dividends, Strategy's Stretch preferred returned about 15-16% and around 20% from IPO, while Bitcoin fell 50% — LeClair's evidence that the instrument successfully strips out 80-90% of Bitcoin volatility.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Empirical proof of product-market fit for volatility-stripped Bitcoin yield — the buyer base is cash parkers, not Bitcoin substitutes.
insights.quote: 12 months in stretch including the dividends is like returned 15 16% or something give or take maybe a little less um now I think it's like 20% from IPO including dividends Bitcoin's down 50.

insights.claim: A perpetual preferred is the structurally correct liability for a permanent Bitcoin holder because it matches infinite asset duration with infinite liability duration, is homogeneous and therefore scalable unlike serial bond issues, and cannot trigger bankruptcy when nothing senior sits above it.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Explains why issuers keep choosing preferreds over cheaper straight debt — and why the preferred is the base layer for further structured products.
insights.quote: the perpetual preferred is the ideal instrument for if you have an infinite duration asset where you don't ever plan to sell it

insights.claim: LeClair says a preferred listed on NASDAQ with an attached shelf ATM is what makes continuous issuance possible — a debt instrument cannot be listed and continuously issued that way, which is why Sailor forgoes the billion-dollar overnight bond raises he could easily do.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: The distribution mechanism, not the coupon, is the real advantage — a template competitors must replicate to scale.
insights.quote: you can't list a debt instrument on the NASDAQ and attach a shelf ATM to it

insights.claim: LeClair concedes the hardcore-Bitcoiner critique that calling preferred equity 'digital credit' is technically wrong, but argues roughly $10 trillion of institutional capital is up for grabs and will never reach Bitcoin unless issuers meet it in the instruments it already buys.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Sizes the incremental demand channel that financialization products are designed to unlock.
insights.quote: there's, you know, about 10 trillion up for grabs and it's never going to come into Bitcoin unless you meet them where they are.

themes.theme: Convert Gamma Squeezing the Preferred Stack

insights.claim: LeClair's mechanical explanation for the preferred selloff: in May Strategy had about $8 billion of convertible bonds at roughly 50 delta, which the market treated as $4bn debt and $4bn future equity; as Bitcoin and MSTR weakened the delta fell toward 20, converting perceived senior debt above the preferreds from ~$3bn to ~$5bn and squeezing the preferreds from both sides.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: The preferred drawdown was a structural repricing of implied seniority, not a solvency event — and it reverses mechanically if MSTR rallies and delta rises again.
insights.quote: In May, when Stretch was firing on all cylinders, you know, there was about 8 billion of convertible bonds and they had a delta of about 50%.

insights.claim: Convertible arbitrage desks trading gamma on Strategy's converts have no view on Bitcoin or MSTR — they sell into strength and buy into weakness — and that gamma transmits directly into the preferred price, which is why Strategy is prioritizing retiring the converts to end up with a Strive-like capital structure.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Gives a watchable catalyst: convert retirement should structurally reduce preferred volatility and lift prices toward par.
insights.quote: it's not so much a weight as it's like this big pendulum that swings back and forth

insights.claim: Strategy's sale of 3,000 Bitcoin around $60K — after which the market went up — destroyed the long-held assumption that any Saylor selling would send Bitcoin to zero, and signaled to rating agencies that the balance sheet, not perpetual stock issuance, can fund dividends.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Removes a key overhang narrative on both Bitcoin and the preferred stack; watch rating-agency treatment as the follow-through.
insights.quote: they sold 3,000 Bitcoin at like 60K. The market went up, right?

insights.claim: LeClair expects the preferreds to self-heal back toward par over months to quarters as a 24-month dividend reserve, multi-year runway and fortress balance sheet get recognized — noting a 12% coupon at a price of 87 is a ~14% yield plus 15% of price upside.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: A stated total-return math for the preferred trade with an explicit multi-quarter timeline.
insights.quote: it's a 12% yield, but it's trading at 87. It's like a 14% yield. Never mind going from 87 to 100 is another 15%.

insights.claim: Responding to Lyn Alden's warning about leverage stacking on preferreds, LeClair argues the endgame should not be near-zero volatility, because a higher Sharpe ratio directly incentivizes more carry trades and leverage — some price discovery and float is healthier.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive risk-management point: excessive stability in these instruments breeds the exact cascading-liquidation risk it appears to eliminate.
insights.quote: the higher the sharp, the more incentive there is to put on carry trades and leverage

themes.theme: Quantum as a Left-Tail Perception Trade

insights.claim: LeClair argues the actual risk from quantum computing to Bitcoin is far lower than the perceived risk, and that the value of the newly announced Bitcoin security consortium is eliminating an unquantifiable left-tail fear that keeps institutional capital on the sidelines.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Frames the consortium as a potential re-rating catalyst via risk-premium compression rather than a technical fix.
insights.quote: the the risk of quantum is far lower than the perception of the risk

insights.claim: LeClair's precedent for the perception trade: Bitcoin re-rated hard after Trump's election not because the administration was bullish but because the left-tail risk of a US government ban was eliminated.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: A reusable model for pricing catalysts — buy the removal of unquantifiable tail risk, not the arrival of good news.
insights.quote: So I would argue that Bitcoin rerated so hard after the election, not because the administration was so bullish and so good for Bitcoin.

insights.claim: In a week of institutional meetings around MetaPlanet's September $1.4 billion public offering — roughly 12 investors a day, with 80 participating — quantum risk was raised unprompted at the end of nearly every meeting.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Firsthand evidence that quantum fear is a live allocation blocker for institutions, making its resolution a demand unlock.
insights.quote: we talked to, I don't know, 12 institutional investors a day for for a week straight. And 80 of those institutional investors participated.

insights.claim: Despite a self-imposed no-price-targets rule since a failed 2021 call, LeClair states his opinion that the Bitcoin bottom is in, pointing to peak hysteria over Saylor selling 800,000 coins and consecutive weeks of ETF outflows.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: A dated, explicit bottom call from an operator with visibility into the shareholder register — falsifiable and worth tracking.
insights.quote: but I would say in in my opinion, I think the bottom's in.

insights.claim: LeClair says Bitcoin and Bitcoin-linked equities bottomed on the exact day of second-quarter close because hedge funds dumped Bitcoin exposure and bought AI and memory names to window-dress the 13F snapshot, and prices have been positive since.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Identifies a calendar-driven, non-fundamental seller whose absence should let Bitcoin names re-rate — and predicts the same hot money rotates back in.
insights.quote: they buy the AI stocks and then the the screenshot comes out

insights.claim: LeClair's bottoming template, drawn from late 2022 when Bitcoin ran from 15 to 23 with no news: capitulation exhausts sellers, two to five months of extremely boring price action follows, then a 26% day arrives with no catalyst.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete pattern and timeline for positioning ahead of the next impulse move rather than waiting for a catalyst.
insights.quote: It's like there's no sellers left

insights.claim: Host Natalie Brunell is more bearish near-term than LeClair, saying she does not yet see what would spark the run, and cites a live prediction-market poll where 58% expect Bitcoin below $55,000 this year and 41% below $50,000.
insights.speaker: Natalie Brunell, host
insights.so_what: Prediction-market positioning gives a concrete distribution of downside expectations against which LeClair's bottom call can be traded.
insights.quote: 58% of people say below 55,000 and 41% say below 50,000 this year

insights.claim: MetaPlanet's stock is down roughly 80% from its 2024 peak to 250 yen — still 12.5x the 20 yen level where the Bitcoin strategy began — and LeClair notes it had already survived an 80% drawdown between July and August 2024, with roughly 100 vol versus Bitcoin's 50.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Calibrates the volatility profile: expect ~2x Bitcoin's realized vol in both directions when sizing positions in MetaPlanet.
insights.quote: We're it's down 80% from 100x in 15 months, right? So the stock's 250 yen. We started the business strategy when the stock was 20 yen

insights.claim: LeClair says every other Japanese Bitcoin treasury company that followed MetaPlanet has now stopped, apologized and abandoned the strategy, leaving MetaPlanet as the sole committed operator in the market.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Competitive-landscape clearing — MetaPlanet inherits the entire Japanese Bitcoin-treasury franchise if the cycle turns.
insights.quote: all of the Bitcoin kind of companies in Japan that have sort of followed us have come out, stopped, they've apologized, and they've said we won't we we're we're done with this business.

insights.claim: MetaPlanet deliberately resisted first-and-second-quarter investor pressure to add leverage, and LeClair says being at 20% leverage rather than 50% when Bitcoin fell to 60K is the controllable variable that preserved the company.
insights.speaker: Dylan LeClair
insights.so_what: Leverage ratio is the single most useful survivability metric for screening Bitcoin treasury companies in a drawdown.
insights.quote: it doesn't feel good when Bitcoin goes to 60K, but it feels it feels better when your leverage is 20% at that point than 50%.
